title: Understanding the cortisol response to stress and improving steroid doses during stress for children with adrenal insufficiency
official: Hydrocortisone administration in stress: a targeted evidence-based approach (HASTE study)
summary:
Background and study aims
When we are ill or under stress, our bodies normally produce extra cortisol, a hormone that helps us cope with stress and recover from illness.

Some children and young people have a condition called adrenal insufficiency, which means their bodies cannot produce enough cortisol. They need to take a medicine called hydrocortisone everyday to replace this hormone. During illness or physical stress, they may need extra hydrocortisone, known as "sick-day doses".

However, there is limited evidence about which types of illness or stress require extra hydrocortisone and how much should be given. Too little hydrocortisone can lead to an adrenal crisis, a potentially life-threatening medical emergency, while too much hydrocortisone, especially if used more often than needed, may affect long-term heart and bone health.

This study aims to better understand how cortisol levels change in children and young people during common illnesses and stressful situations, including fever, vomiting or diarrhoea, vaccinations and school examinations.

The natural cortisol response to stress will be compared with the levels seen in children with adrenal insufficiency taking the currently recommended sick-day doses of hydrocortisone.

The findings will help to identify hydrocortisone doses that more closely match the body's natural response to stress, with the aim of improving future sick-day dosing guidance.

Who can participate?
Children and young people aged 6 months to 18 years may be able to participate. The study involves two parts, with different groups of participants.

Part 1 includes children and young people who do not have adrenal insufficiency and are facing one of four common stressors: fever, vomiting or diarrhoea, childhood vaccinations or GCSE mock examinations.

Part 2 includes children and young people with adrenal insufficiency who take hydrocortisone medication normally.

What does the study involve?
Part 1: Understanding the body’s healthy response to stress in children and young people
Children and young people without adrenal insufficiency will collect saliva samples when they are facing one of four stressful situations: unwell with a fever, or diarrhoea or vomiting, getting a vaccination or having a mock GCSE examination.

They will give one sample when joining the study, five samples the following day (during stress), and five more when they have recovered. This allows us to compare each child's cortisol and cortisone levels during stress with their usual levels when they are well. They can collect the saliva samples at home, and then return them by prepaid post. 

Part 2: Measuring the cortisol response to current sick day doses in children with adrenal insufficiency
Children and young people with adrenal insufficiency will take the currently recommended sick day doses of medicine, but on a day when they feel well.
Participants will provide saliva samples to help us understand how saliva cortisol and cortisone levels change after taking hydrocortisone. Their cortisol and cortisone levels will be compared with the natural stress responses measured in Part 1. This will help to understand how closely the current sick-day doses match the body’s usual response to stress.
Some children and young people will also give blood samples too. A lot is already known about how hydrocortisone affects cortisol levels in the blood, but less is known about how it changes cortisol and cortisone levels in saliva. Collecting both blood and saliva samples from some people will help us understand the relationship between these measurements. This will allow us to make the best use of both the new information collected in this study and the information already available.

Part 3: Developing better doses
The research team will use the information collected in Parts 1 and 2 to develop a computer model that predicts how different hydrocortisone doses affect cortisol levels.

The model will help identify sick-day dosing regimens that most closely match the body's natural cortisol response during different illnesses and stressful situations.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may not benefit directly from taking part in this study. Instead, it is hoped that the findings could help improve sick-day hydrocortisone dosing guidance for children and young people with adrenal insufficiency in the future. This may help reduce the risk of adrenal crisis while avoiding unnecessarily high doses of hydrocortisone.

This study is very low risk. Collecting saliva samples can feel a bit strange at first but is very safe. The samples can be collected at home to avoid any extra hospital visits. 

In Part 2, children with adrenal insufficiency will take their sick-day doses of hydrocortisone on a day when they are well. This is considered low risk because side effects from taking too much hydrocortisone are more likely when higher doses are taken repeatedly or over a long time. In this study, children will only take these higher doses for one day.

Where is the study run from?
The HASTE study is based at Alder Hey Children's Hospital in Liverpool, UK, and our partner primary care sites.  It is sponsored by the University of Liverpool, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
November 2026 to September 2029.

Who is funding the study?
A National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Doctoral Award and a charitable donation to the University of Liverpool, UK.

Who is the main contact?

Prof Joanne Blair, jo.blair@alderhey.nhs.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Adrenal-sufficient CYP (Part 1)
1. CYP aged 6 months to 18 years
2. Presenting to Alder Hey Children’s Hospital (AHCH) or primary care (PC24, Vauxhall Medical Practice) with one of the following predefined stressors:
2.1. Acute stress: 
2.1.1. Fever > = 37.5°C and deemed clinically significant, measured at home on a digital thermometer or by a healthcare provider within the last 24 hours
2.1.2. Vomiting and/or diarrhoea (with or without fever)
2.2. Routine stress: 
2.2.1. Vaccination at a partner GP practice; or 
2.2.2. Mock GCSE examination at a partner school

AI CYP (Part 2)
1. Age 6 months – 18 years
2. Confirmed diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency, including autoimmune and congenital causes (e.g., Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia [CAH])
Exclusion criteria:
Adrenal-sufficient CYP (Part 1)
1. Outside of stated age-range
2. Oral conditions that may cause blood contamination of saliva samples (e.g., gingivitis, mouth ulcers, recent dental procedures)
3. Current glucocorticoid therapy or use of any glucocorticoid therapy in the the last 3 months (table 1). Where a participant is found to have been commenced on such a medication after recruitment, they will be excluded from the study.
4. Diagnosis of Cushing’s Disease or other condition known to be associated with disruption of cortisol physiology
5. For participants recruited under routine stress cohorts (vaccination or mock examination): presence of fever > = 37.5°C measured by a digital thermometer at home or at healthcare provider and deemed clinically significant or vomiting/diarrhoea in the 24 hours prior to the index stressor

AI CYP (Parts 2)
1. Outside of stated age-range
2. Oral conditions that may cause blood contamination of saliva
3. Intercurrent illness at time of proposed sample collection
4. Current use of glucocorticoids beyond those required for adrenal insufficiency or medications affecting glucocorticoid metabolism. Where a participant is found to have been commenced on such a medication after recruitment, they will be excluded from the study.
